title: Exceptions for rejects
text: Pattern seven: exceptions for rejected orders. Validation that throws is the textbook way to report bad input. On this box, the happy path barely notices. But every rejected order costs about one and a half microseconds.

title: The general version
text: Here is the general version. validate checks the quantity and the price band, and throws a std::runtime_error with a message when either is wrong. on_order wraps the call in try, records the reason in the catch block, and otherwise sends the order. This is clean, correct C++. Errors cannot be ignored, and the happy path reads as if there were none.

title: What a throw costs
text: Modern exceptions are called zero cost: when nothing throws, the happy path runs no extra instructions. The unwind information sits in tables, off to the side. The cost moves to the throw. First the message: to_string and a concatenation, then runtime_error copies the text to the heap. Then the runtime allocates the exception object, and the unwinder starts. It searches up the stack, reading the unwind tables of each frame, until it finds a matching catch. Then it walks the frames again, running cleanups, and lands in the handler. Measured here: one and a half microseconds per rejected order.

title: The hot-path version
text: The hot-path version treats a reject as an ordinary result, because at a busy gateway it is one. check returns a small enum: none, bad quantity, or bad price. Each failing branch is marked unlikely, so the accept path is laid out as straight-line code that falls through. on_order tests the code once. On a reject it calls reject, marked cold and noinline, so the formatting lives far away from the hot instructions. It writes the same text as the general version, so nothing downstream changes. In C++23, std::expected carries a value or an error in the same way.

title: Measured
text: Measured on this box: four hundred thousand orders, pinned to one core, five runs. With no rejects, the two are close: 3.2 nanoseconds per order against 2.7. Zero cost really is close to zero. With one order in a hundred rejected, the general version averaged 40 nanoseconds per order, against 2.9. Its p99 jumped to 1.4 microseconds, against 61 nanoseconds, because every reject lands in the tail. And the hot function went from 49 instructions to 28, with the accept path just sixteen, and no call.

title: When it's fine
text: Exceptions are not slow in general. For truly exceptional events, like a lost connection or a bad config at startup, throwing is the right tool. The missing constraint is the reject rate. At a gateway, rejects are routine traffic, so they belong in the return type. State the expected reject rate, and measure p99 with rejects mixed in, not just the happy path. The rule: throw for the exceptional, return codes for the expected.
